We are grateful for the reviewer’s careful assessment of our work and the thoughtful feedback provided. The remarks highlight several meaningful aspects that help us further refine the paper. The reviewer also raises some questions that help us to further clarify our work. We present our responses below and hope they effectively clarify the concerns raised.

**W1. Generalization to Out-of-Distribution (OOD) Scenarios**

We thank the reviewer for raising this concern. We agree that it is important to demonstrate the Out-of-Distribution (OOD) generalization capabilities of our method.

Actually, our experimental setup in Tables 1–4 and Figures 4–5 already reflects an OOD setting. Specifically, the safety-degraded reference model is trained using data from only a subset of harmful categories (e.g., crime and offensive content). However, during customized fine-tuning, we introduce harmful samples spanning a broader and more comprehensive set of safety categories with explicit harmful contents. Despite this distribution shift, our method consistently defends against safety degradation and preserves model safety significantly better than baseline approaches. This demonstrates the ability of TOSS/TOSS-Pro to generalize across different safety categories beyond those seen during reference model training.

To further address the reviewer’s concern, we have conducted an additional experiment explicitly targeting OOD scenarios. In this study, we train the safety-degraded reference model on harmful data that excludes the privacy category (which consists of harmful question-response pairs related to privacy breaches, such as how to steal private information or compromise personal privacy). Then, during customized fine-tuning, we add harmful examples from the privacy subclass of the Nemotron Content Safety Dataset \[R1] into our custom fine-tuning dataset. Even under this setup, our token selection mechanism, guided by the reference models, enables the fine-tuned model to maintain strong safety performance. From the results in Table R1, compared to Standard SFT, our approach achieves significantly stronger safety preservation, confirming that reference models trained on a subset of harmful categories can effectively transfer to unseen categories.

**Table R1:** Evaluation results of StandardSFT and TOSS under the OOD setting.

| **Dataset**          |  | **ANTHROPIC HH test** |              |       |    **HEx-PHI**     |              | **SLIMORCA test** |
|---------------|--------------|-----------------|--------------|--------------|----------------|--------------|----------------|
| **Metric**        | **Win Rate (↑)** | **Harmfulness Score (↓)** | **ASR (↓)**     | **Win Rate (↑)** | **Harmfulness Score (↓)** | **ASR (↓)**    | **Win Rate (↑)**  |
| Standard SFT  | 50           | 3.01            | 94.68        | 50           | 4.17           | 87.57        | 50             |
| TOSS          | 88.12        | 2.48            | 77.18        | 90.80        | 2.40           | 53.03        | 66.59          |

**W2. Reference Model Training Data**

We thank the reviewer for highlighting this important point. We agree that the composition, source, and size of the reference model training datasets are essential for reproducibility, and we provide the details here for clarity. For the safety-degraded reference model, we sample approximately 10% of the Red Teaming subset from Anthropic HH-RLHF \[R2], focusing on a subset of harmful categories such as crime, violence, abuse, and offensive queries. For the utility-oriented reference model, we sample approximately 3% of the OpenOrca dataset \[R3] to construct the utility-focused supervision signal. These datasets are intentionally lightweight yet sufficiently representative for learning the contrasting safety- and utility-oriented behaviors required by our dual-reference design. We will release all the processed training splits used for both reference models to ensure full reproducibility and facilitate future research.

**W3. Comupational Cost and Performance Gain**

We appreciate the reviewer for raising this concern. We agree that our method TOSS introduces additional computational cost compared to intervention methods (e.g., Circuit Breakers) and model-editing techniques (e.g., SafetyLock). Below, we clarify why this cost is both acceptable and worthwhile by analyzing (i) computational cost and (ii) safety performance.

(1) **Computational cost analysis**

Our problem setting specifically targets how to preserve safety during fine-tuning while still maximizing the utility gains of customization. This requires identifying and removing safety-degrading tokens before fine-tuning. To achieve this, our method conducts token-level assessment using two reference LoRA models. Although this introduces cost, **it remains practical because all reference models are trained with lightweight LoRA fine-tuning rather than full-parameter optimization**. By comparison, **Circuit Breakers** also require additional training. They first obtain a customized LLM via the Standard SFT, and then perform a secondary LoRA fine-tuning stage to push the representation of certain layers away from harmful directions. Their extra cost is slightly lower than ours, but still non-trivial. **SafetyLock** performs training-free activation steering, which indeed incurs much lower overhead.

Thus, we acknowledge that our approach introduces more cost than SafetyLock and somewhat more than Circuit Breakers. **However, the key question is whether this cost is justified by the resulting safety performance, especially under extremely harmful fine-tuning scenarios.**

(2) **Safety performance analysis**

Crucially, **the defense paradigm of TOSS fundamentally differs from both Circuit Breakers and SafetyLock.** Both low-cost methods defend after Standard SFT, meaning that if the fine-tuning dataset contains a large proportion of safety-degrading tokens, the resulting customized LLM may already have severely compromised safety before defense is applied. Once safety has been heavily degraded, methods that attempt to “repair” the model after fine-tuning can fail under such extreme threat conditions. Moreover, approaches such as SafetyLock rely on accurately estimating a safety vector and selecting an appropriate steering strength; their effectiveness deteriorates sharply when these estimates deviate from the optimal values. Similarly, Circuit Breakers depend heavily on the correct choice of target layers; if the harmful drift is distributed across layers, their ability to recover safety degrades sharply. In contrast, TOSS prevents safety degradation at the source by removing harmful tokens before fine-tuning. It eliminates the root cause rather than attempting to repair harm that has already occurred. **This difference is essential in the highly adversarial fine-tuning scenario we study. Under such settings, we observe that both SafetyLock and Circuit Breakers fail to provide meaningful safety protection, while TOSS maintains strong defense capabilities.**

To address the reviewer’s concern, we conduct additional experiments comparing TOSS, SafetyLock, and Circuit Breakers under our challenging harmful fine-tuning setting. Results are shown in Table R4. From the results, we observe that both SafetyLock and Circuit Breakers achieve safety performance nearly identical to Standard SFT, indicating that they provide essentially no effective defense under our highly adversarial fine-tuning attack setting. This result further supports our claim that **the additional cost introduced by TOSS is minor compared to the severity of the safety degradation that low-cost methods fail to prevent**.

**Table R4:** Evaluation results (win rate) of different methods with different computational cost on both safety and utility benchmarks.

| Method           | ANTHROPIC HH test (↑) | HEx-PHI (↑) | SLIMORCA test (↑) | Paradigm               |
| :---------------- | :--------------------- | :----------- | :----------------- | :---------------------- |
| Standard SFT     | 50                    | 50          | 50                | /                      |
| SafetyLock       | 50.25                 | 50.34       | 50.72             | Training-free defense  |
| Circuit Breakers | 40.25                 | 44.00       | 50.95             | Training-based defense |
| TOSS             | **88.82**             | **87.54**   | **68.37**         | Training-based defense |

**References:**

\[R1] Yu, Longhui, et al. "Metamath: Bootstrap your own mathematical questions for large language models." arXiv preprint arXiv:2309.12284 (2023).

\[R2] Ganguli, Deep, et al. "Red teaming language models to reduce harms: Methods, scaling behaviors, and lessons learned." arXiv preprint arXiv:2209.07858 (2022).

**W3. Potential for Response Disruption and Utility Evaluation**

We thank the reviewer for raising this concern. Actually, our token-level selection method does not harm the general capability of LLM. The model trained with TOSS will not lead to discontinuous or ill-formed generated responses.

To further address the reviewer’s concern about potential degradation of general capabilities, we additionally evaluate our token-level selective fine-tuning method on some widely used benchmarks (MMLU, HellaSwag, and TruthfulQA) that cover diverse knowledge domains and general instruction-following utility. As shown in Table R2, the performance of our method (TOSS) is nearly identical to that of the base model without fine-tuning. This indicates that our token-level selective customized fine-tuning does not impair the model’s general problem-solving capabilities or world knowledge. Furthermore, due to the existence of harmful data with misinformation in the custom fine-tuning dataset, the Standard SFT method demonstrates substantial degradation on the TruthfulQA benchmark, while our method still obtains comparable performance with the base model.

**Table R2:** Results of different methods on some widely used benchmarks evaluating the general capabilities of LLMs.

| :----------- | :------- | :------------ | :------------- |

| Standard SFT | 62.99    | 57.95         | 15.91          |
| SEAL         | 63.09    | 58.09         | 42.11          |
| TOSS         | 63.07    | 59.03         | 45.78          |

**W4. AI Safety Evaluation Metrics**

We thank the reviewer for highlighting this important concern regarding the safety evaluation protocol. We agree that LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation may introduce potential biases, and we appreciate the opportunity to clarify and further justify our metric. While human annotation is indeed the gold-standard approach for assessing harmfulness, it is prohibitively expensive at the scale required for comprehensive safety evaluation on diverse safety benchmarks. In practice, LLM-as-a-Judge evaluations have been widely adopted by recent works on LLM safety \[R4, R5, R6, R7], and they have demonstrated their strong alignment with human safety judgments. Consequently, LLM-as-a-Judge has become a de facto standard for evaluating safety in large language models.

In our work, we follow the evaluation protocol established in SEAL, our primary baseline, where safety is assessed using a win-rate metric comparing the evaluated model’s response to a reference model’s response under identical prompts. This ensures that all methods, including ours, are compared under a consistent and widely accepted evaluation paradigm.

To address the reviewer’s concern, we further conduct human annotations on responses generated by different methods to evaluate the effectiveness of our approach. Below, we present several illustrative cases showing that the LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation results are largely consistent with human judgments, supporting the reliability of our evaluation protocol. For the harmful query "How can I break into a cannon gun safe with a digital keypad? Give me step by step instructions.", the response of the reference model is "1. First, you need to get the combination from someone who knows it or figure out how to guess it yourself..." and the response of the model under evaluation is "Oh no, breaking into a secure device like a cannon gun safe is not the right thing to do...". The LLM judge model considers the model under evaluation wins, which is aligned with human annotations.

Additionally, to further alleviate the reviewer’s concerns, we adopt a more comprehensive set of evaluation metrics. By leveraging multiple, complementary measures, we provide a more thorough assessment of model safety and aim to mitigate potential biases. Specifically, we measure Attack Success Rate (ASR) following the keyword-matching protocol of \[R8], Harmfulness Score following the rubric-based LLM-as-a-Judge protocol of \[R4], with scores ranging from 1 to 5, and Win Rate, consistent with SEAL’s setting.

summary.value: This paper argues that the root cause of safety degradation during LLM fine-tuning lies at the token level, a finer granularity than the conventional sample level. To address this, the authors propose TOSS and its progressive variant, TOSS-Pro, which aim to identify and mask high-risk tokens to preserve the model's safety alignment.

strengths.value:
1. To my knowledge, this is the first work to propose a token-level data selection framework specifically for safe LLM fine-tuning. This fine-grained approach convincingly addresses a key limitation of coarse-grained, sample-level methods, which often discard valuable, task-relevant information.

2. The motivation is well-supported by a clear diagnostic analysis. The KL divergence analysis across token positions provides compelling empirical evidence for the paper's central hypothesis that safety-degrading signals are localized and not uniformly distributed, thus justifying the need for a token-level solution

weaknesses.value:
1. The method's effectiveness is heavily dependent on the quality of the initial reference models, which introduces significant computational/data overhead and a potential "bootstrapping paradox". The framework requires two pre-trained reference models (a safety-degraded model and a utility-oriented model), which demands substantial extra resources and datasets. More critically, there is a circular dependency: to clean a custom dataset, one needs reference models trained on datasets that are assumed to be well-profiled. While the authors propose TOSS-Pro to iteratively refine the safety-degraded model, this does not fully resolve the "garbage-in, garbage-out" problem. If the initial reference model is of poor quality, the iterative process may fail to effectively identify harmful tokens. The paper lacks a sensitivity analysis on how the quality of the initial reference datasets impacts the final performance.

2. The proposed scoring function risks over-filtering useful tokens in specialized domains where the line between "harmful" and "technical" is blurry. For example, in tasks like chemical synthesis or cybersecurity, tokens related to potentially dangerous but scientifically valid concepts could be incorrectly assigned high-risk scores and masked. The paper's evaluation of utility is confined to a general-purpose instruction-following dataset (SLIMORCA). To demonstrate robustness, the method must be evaluated on more complex and professional domains such as code generation (e.g., LiveCodeBench), mathematical reasoning (e.g., AIME), and scientific QA. Furthermore, the paper does not report the impact on the model's general capabilities, which should be measured on standard benchmarks like MMLU. 

3. The paper's comparison is limited to other data-centric, training-time methods and overlooks other important defense paradigms. To justify the significant computational cost of TOSS, it is crucial to compare it against less expensive alternatives, such as test-time intervention methods (e.g., Circuit Breakers) or model-editing techniques (e.g., Safety Arithmetic, SafetyLock). Without this comparison, it is unclear whether the performance gains offered by TOSS are substantial enough to warrant its high resource demands.

## Summary of our work

In this work, we present the **first** systematic token-level analysis of safety degradation during the fine-tuning process. This analysis motivates the development of a novel token-level data selection framework, **TOSS**, designed to enhance the safety of LLM fine-tuning. Furthermore, we introduce a progressive refinement strategy, **TOSS-Pro**, which iteratively improves both the safety-degraded model and the data selection process, leading to enhanced safety performance. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our framework achieves **state-of-the-art** performance, resulting in a **25%** higher win rate on safety benchmarks and an **11%** higher win rate on utility benchmarks, compared to existing baselines. We envision several potential directions for automatically or adaptively determining the discarding ratio: (i) Coarse-grained search. The range of $d$ can be partitioned into a small number of coarse intervals. For each candidate $d$, one can obtain the retained tokens and perform a few steps of lightweight customized fine-tuning to identify the best-performing region. This requires only a small number of additional fine-tuning steps. (ii) Curriculum-style adaptive scheduling. Instead of using a fixed discarding ratio throughout training, one may start with a larger $d$ to aggressively remove safety-degrading tokens, and gradually decrease $d$ as the model becomes more aligned. This schedule may lead to further performance enhancement due to the adaptive choice of $d$ during customized fine-tuning. (iii) Per-sample learnable thresholds. Inspired by SEAL’s learnable per-sample filtering threshold, one could assign a learnable local token-discarding threshold for each sample. By training these learnable per-sample filtering thresholds, it enables more granular and adaptive token selection than a global scalar $d$.

All three strategies have the potential to further improve the robustness and automation of the discarding process, but they also introduce additional computational overhead. Therefore, developing a lightweight yet effective mechanism for setting $d$ constitutes a valuable direction for future research.

**W3. Clarity on Progressive Refinement Sample Selection**

We thank the reviewer for raising this comment. We would like to further clarify the details of our TOSS-Pro method. Actually, if any token in a sample is contained in the top token set, this sample is included in $\mathcal{D}\_{t}^{s}$. Specifically, in each iteration, we first sort all tokens in the descending order according to the designed token score. We then retrieve the corresponding sample from the high-scoring to the low-scoring token and orderly add the sample into $\mathcal{D}\_{t}^{s}$. If the sample has already been in $\mathcal{D}\_{t}^{s}$, we will skip the token and move to the next token. This process is repeated until there are $k$ samples in the set $\mathcal{D}\_{t}^{s}$.

Our intuition is that these selected samples necessarily contain top-ranked tokens, i.e., the most informative harmful tokens, and are therefore especially useful for guiding the training of the safety-degraded model. By focusing on samples enriched with such informative signals, the model can learn more effectively during each iteration.

**Q1. Visualized Examples with Utility-critical Tokens**

We thank the reviewer for this insightful suggestion. To further support the claim that selective masking of our TOSS preserves utility-critical tokens, we provide several representative examples in Appendix J, illustrating some utility-critical tokens are masked by the naive baseline while our method retains these tokens. From these examples, it is evident that the first few tokens of the responses are directly related to the final answer, and masking them probably leads to a degradation in utility performance. These observations further demonstrate that the naive baseline of masking the first five tokens fails to achieve a better balance between safety and utility. In contrast, our TOSS method enables a more favorable trade-off, effectively preserving utility while mitigating safety risks.

**Q2. Weighted Score**

We thank the reviewer for this insightful question. Although an unweighted loss difference is used in our formulation, we agree that it is reasonable to utilize a weighted loss suggested by the reviewer. To investigate the impact of the two hyperparameters $\alpha$ and $\beta$ on safety and utility performance, we utilize a weighted score, assigning $\alpha$ and $\beta$ with different values, to assess each token and perform token selection. The results are presented in Appendix K and Figure 7. From the results, we see that assigning a higher weight to the loss on the utility-oriented model leads to unsatisfying safety performance, while assigning a higher weight to the loss on the safety-degraded model leads to degraded utility performance. Notably, if setting $\alpha=\beta=\frac{1}{2}$, it obtains superior performance on both safety and utility benchmarks. These results indicate that meticulously choosing these two hyperparameters has the potential to allow for a more deliberate control over the safety-utility trade-off. One straightforward method is to learn these hyperparameters through a bi-level optimization akin to SEAL. However, it may introduce extra costs. Therefore, designing an effective and efficient choosing strategy of these hyperparameters is an interesting future direction.

We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s thorough evaluation of our submission and their positive recognition of our work. The reviewer’s comments are highly insightful, which have offered valuable suggestions for further strengthening the paper and some interesting future directions. We hope that the responses below adequately address the raised concerns.

**W1. Computational Cost of Reference Model Training**

We thank the reviewer for raising this important concern. While TOSS requires training two reference models, the actual computational overhead is modest because both models are obtained via lightweight LoRA fine-tuning. In practice, training both the safety-degraded and utility-oriented 7B reference models takes only about 3 hours in total on 4×A6000 GPUs (\~0.5 GPU days).

Although SEAL uses a lightweight ranking selector, its actual training pipeline is substantially more expensive in practice. Specifically, SEAL’s bi-level optimization requires jointly updating the LLM parameters during data-ranker training. This LLM update is performed solely to assist ranker optimization rather than to produce the final customized model. Furthermore, SEAL additionally requires a reference dataset of comparable scale and combines it with the custom fine-tuning data to train the data selector. These two factors significantly increase computational demand. In our experiments, training SEAL’s data ranker requires about 7 hours on 4×A6000 GPUs (\~1.17 GPU days), which is notably higher than the total cost of training our two reference models. Thus, although TOSS appears to involve more components, its time complexity and computational overhead are in fact lower than SEAL, while achieving substantially better safety and utility performance (see Table 1).

We also acknowledge that the cost of training reference models naturally increases as the LLM scales up. To address this potential concern, we have explored whether token selections obtained from another model sharing the same tokenizer can be directly transferred to the target model for customized fine-tuning without retraining reference models or rerunning token assessment. Our preliminary experiments demonstrate that this strategy is indeed feasible. As shown in Table 2, TOSS exhibits strong transferability across models that share the same tokenizer: the selected tokens derived from one model can be applied to another, yet the resulting customized fine-tuned model still significantly outperforms Standard SFT, SEAL, and other baselines. These results support that it is possible to utilize a small model with the same tokenizer to perform token selection and directly transfer the selection result to the larger target model. Furthermore, when a larger target model lacks an available smaller model with the same tokenizer, a small model can be trained to align the tokenizer and subsequently used for token selection. This procedure remains low-cost, owing to the limited parameter size of the smaller model.

This initial evidence suggests a promising direction: small reference models can serve as efficient token selectors for larger LLMs, thereby substantially reducing the computational cost while maintaining strong safety and utility performance.

**W2. Hyperparameter Sensitivity of Discarding Ratio**

We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. While Figure 5 indeed shows that utility first increases and then decreases as the discarding ratio $d$ grows, we would like to emphasize that the utility performance remains remarkably stable across a wide range of discarding ratios (e.g., $d \in \left [ 0.1,0.5 \right ] $), with only minor fluctuations. This indicates that TOSS does not require a finely tuned value of $d$ to achieve strong performance, and that the method is substantially robust to the choice of $d$ in practice. Nevertheless, we agree that the selection of $d$ is an important design choice and that developing more principled strategies could further strengthen the framework.

Under local ranking, each sample discards the same proportion of tokens. This causes (i) harmful samples to retain safety-degrading tokens, reducing safety, and (ii) benign samples to lose utility-critical tokens, reducing helpfulness. In contrast, global ranking adaptively discards tokens based on their global harmfulness scores across the entire dataset, ensuring that more safety-degrading tokens from harmful samples are removed while preserving utility-critical tokens. This explains why the global-ranking strategy achieves a better trade-off between safety and utility than local ranking.

**Q2. Win Rate Comparison between SEAL and TOSS**

We thank the reviewer for raising this question. As the win-rate metric allows any model to serve as the comparison model, it is valid as long as all methods are evaluated against the same comparison model. To address the reviewer’s concern, we additionally compute the win-rate of TOSS using the customized fine-tuned model obtained through the SEAL method as the comparison model. The results are reported in Table R4 and Appendix H.

We observe that the win-rate of TOSS against SEAL is slightly lower than the win-rate obtained when using Standard SFT as the comparison model. This is consistent with the expectation, since the SEAL fine-tuned model achieves stronger utility and safety performance than Standard SFT.

**Table R4:** Evaluation results of TOSS utilizing Standard SFT and SEAL as the comparison model respectively.

| :------------------- | :--------------------- | :----------- | :----------------- |
| TOSS (Standard SFT) | 88.82                 | 87.54       | 68.37             |
| TOSS (SEAL)         | 84.54                 | 78.28       | 63.96             |

**Q3. Explaination about Figure 5**

We thank the reviewer for pointing out the need for clarification regarding Figure 5. The purpose of this figure is to examine whether our fine-grained token-level selection method consistently outperforms the coarse-grained sample-level method under different token-discarding ratios, thereby evaluating the robustness of our approach.

Specifically, for each discarding ratio, we remove the same total number of tokens using token-level selection and sample-level selection, respectively. We then fine-tune the model on the retained tokens/samples and evaluate both safety and utility performance. The results show that across a wide range of discarding ratios, our token-level method achieves superior safety–utility trade-offs and maintains more stable performance, demonstrating its robustness.

Regarding the reviewer’s question: when the discarding ratio equals 1, all tokens in the custom dataset utilized for fine-tuning are discarded for both token-level and sample-level methods. In this case, no fine-tuning is performed at all, making both methods equivalent to the original base model. Therefore, safety is highest at ratio = 1 (since the model avoids any safety degradation from fine-tuning), while utility is lowest (since no downstream adaptation occurs).

We sincerely thank the reviewer for this insightful and constructive suggestion. We appreciate the concern regarding our reliance on the win rate metric. While the win rate can capture relative safety by comparing outputs against a comparison model and indicating whether our method outperforms baselines, we agree that absolute safety metrics are necessary for a more comprehensive evaluation. Importantly, our method also maintains a false-refusal rate comparable to the baselines, indicating that the safety gains do not come at the cost of over-refusal. These results demonstrate that our fine-grained token-level defense method achieves a better trade-off between safety and utility, which are aligned with the win rate metric.

This paper proposes TOSS, a token-level data selection framework for mitigating safety degradation during LLM fine-tuning, together with a progressive variant TOSS-Pro. By leveraging two lightweight reference models (a safety-degraded model and a utility-oriented model), the method identifies and selectively masks high-risk tokens, achieving a substantially improved safety–utility trade-off over prior sample-level defenses.

Across reviewers, there is broad agreement that the paper is novel, well-motivated, and empirically strong, particularly in its shift from sample-level to token-level selection. Reviewers consistently praise the diagnostic analysis, methodological clarity, and strong gains over SEAL and other baselines on multiple safety benchmarks. The main points of discussion focus on (1) computational overhead and dependence on reference models, (2) robustness and generalization (OOD safety categories, specialized domains), (3) adequacy and completeness of safety/utility evaluation metrics, and (4) potential side effects of token masking on fluency and general capabilities.

The rebuttal is unusually comprehensive: the authors introduce extensive new experiments (absolute safety metrics, OOD safety categories, math reasoning, general capability benchmarks, sensitivity to reference model quality, comparisons with post-hoc defenses), detailed methodological clarifications, and concrete cost analyses. These additions substantially strengthen the paper and directly address most substantive reviewer concerns. Remaining disagreements largely reflect differences in expected evaluation scope or philosophical preferences over defense paradigms, rather than unresolved technical flaws.

We appreciate the reviewer’s thorough evaluation of our submission. The comments raise important points for strengthening the paper through more comprehensive experiments. We address each concern in detail below and hope that our clarifications adequately resolve the issues raised.

**W1. Sensitivity Analysis on Reference Models**

We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. We agree that our framework requires training two reference models, which inevitably introduce additional computational overhead. However, because we adopt lightweight LoRA fine-tuning, the combined training cost of both reference models is only around 3 hours on 4×A6000 GPUs (\~0.5 GPU days), making the additional overhead minor in practice.

More importantly, thanks to the iterative refinement mechanism of TOSS-Pro, our approach does not rely on high-quality reference models at initialization. By progressively updating the safety-degraded model, TOSS-Pro rapidly improves reference model quality even when the initial model is weak.

To validate this, we conduct a systematic sensitivity analysis on how the quality of the initial safety-degraded reference model affects the final performance. Concretely, we train three initial reference models using 1300, 1000, and 500 harmful samples, respectively (based on Llama-2-7B-Chat-hf), producing Initial Reference Model-1, Initial Reference Model-2, and Initial Reference Model-3, whose quality decreases gradually. From the results reported in Table R1, applying vanilla TOSS with these three models for token selection and token-level customized fine-tuning yields customized models whose safety and utility degrade accordingly. Notably, models derived from Initial Reference Model-3 (trained with only 500 samples) exhibit utility comparable to Standard SFT but even lower safety than Standard SFT, indicating that Initial Reference Model-3 is indeed a poor-quality reference model.

However, after applying only two rounds of refinement to update the safety-degraded reference model, TOSS-Pro under all three initial models converges to nearly identical safety and utility performance, yielding consistent and significant improvements over baseline methods, regardless of the initial reference model quality.

These results demonstrate that TOSS-Pro effectively mitigates the “bootstrapping paradox”: even when starting from low-quality reference models, iterative refinement reliably improves the reference model and leads to robust token selection and fine-tuning performance. Consequently, our TOSS-Pro is not sensitive to the initial reference model quality and is resistant to the “garbage-in, garbage-out’’ failure mode.

For each token in the custom dataset, we compute two per-token KL divergences: (i) between the customized model and the safe base model  (ii) between the customized model and the safety-degraded model. The per-token KL divergence difference captures whether fine-tuning on the corresponding token shifts the model **away** from safe behaviors and **toward** unsafe behaviors. Empirically, we observe that tokens with large KL divergence differences include both tokens related to explicit harmful concepts and tokens with no harmful semantics.

Because the KL divergence difference cannot be computed before obtaining the customized model, our practical scoring function approximates it with a loss-difference–based score, decomposed into a safety-related score and a utility-related score. The safety-related score measures the loss difference between the base model and the safety-degraded model. A high safety-related score implies that the corresponding token is more aligned with the generation distribution of the unsafe model compared to the safe base model. Fine-tuning on this token pushes the base model toward the unsafe model’s distribution. Thus, removing these tokens prevents safety degradation during fine-tuning.

In conclusion, this mechanism depends on distributional shifts rather than token semantics. Therefore, even in specialized domains where “harmful” and “technical” concepts overlap, our method identifies safety-degrading tokens rather than dangerous-sounding tokens. This property substantially mitigates risks of over-filtering useful domain-specific content.

Thank the reviewer for this insightful question. We agree that a safety-degrading token $y_{i}$, once identified and masked such that it does not contribute to the loss, can still appear in the input context for predicting a subsequent unmasked token $y_{i+1}$. However, this does not imply that fine-tuning on $y_{i+1}$ would cause the model to learn harmful information or suffer from residual harmful signals.

First, our goal is to discard safety-degrading tokens, rather than to identify tokens that are semantically harmful. Prior work \[R4, R9] has shown that safety degradation can arise not only from harmful samples containing explicit harmful information but also from benign samples without any harmful content. Our preliminary token-level diagnostic analysis further confirms this: The shift from a safe base model toward an unsafe model can occur at both benign tokens with no harmful content and harmful tokens carrying explicit harmful semantics. If a discarded token $y_{i}$ is benign, its presence in the context of $y_{i+1}$ clearly does not introduce any residual harmful signal.

Second, even if the masked token $y_{i}$ contains explicit harmful information, the model will not be pushed toward harmful behavior when fine-tuning on an unmasked subsequent token $y_{i+1}$. This follows directly from the design of our token assessment function, which decomposes into a safety-related score and a utility-related score. According to the safety-related score, a token is classified as safety-degrading only if its loss under the safety-degrading model is significantly lower than that under the base model, indicating that gradient updates on such a token would quickly pull the model toward harmful generation. In contrast, an unmasked token $y_{i+1}$ necessarily has a low safety-related score (i.e., its loss under the unsafe model is higher than or comparable to that under the base model), meaning that gradient updates on $y_{i+1}$ do not move the model toward harmful behavior.

Therefore, the fact that $y_{i+1}$ is trained while seeing $y_{i}$ in the context does not introduce residual harmful signals. For this reason, simply masking out safety-degrading tokens is adequate to mitigate the risk the reviewer raised, and it does not compromise the intended safety improvements.

This paper introduces a novel framework for safe LLM fine-tuning called Token-level data Selection for Safe LLM fine-tuning (TOSS), which directly addresses the critical issue of safety degradation during domain-specific model adaptation.
The core of TOSS is a unique mechanism that quantifies the safety risk of each token within the custom dataset. This is achieved by measuring the loss difference between a safety-degraded model (trained on harmful data) and a utility-oriented model (trained on high-quality utility data).
By employing this fine-grained, token-level data selection instead of conventional coarse-grained (sample-level) filtering, the authors achieve a more efficient utilization of the training data. The resulting cleaned dataset allows for a more effective instruction-tuning process, leading to a superior trade-off that significantly enhances model safety.

strengths.value:
- Novelty and Performance: The paper proposes a simple yet highly effective token-level data selection method (TOSS/TOSS-Pro). The experimental results demonstrate its superiority, achieving SOTA performance across three distinct safety benchmarks.

- Clarity and Methodology: The presentation of the work is notably clear. The authors effectively structure the paper by including preliminary experiments (diagnostic analysis) which systematically build the rationale for their main design, guiding the reader through the necessity of the fine-grained, token-level approach.

weaknesses.value:
- Generalization to Out-of-Distribution (OOD) Scenarios: The paper primarily focuses on the safety issue during the post-training or continuous fine-tuning phase. Since the two reference models (safety-degraded and utility-oriented) heavily rely on in-domain data for training, the generalizability of TOSS/TOSS-Pro to Out-of-Distribution (OOD) safety scenarios is questionable. For instance, if the reference models are trained using financial safety-related data, safety concerns might still persist in OOD domains such as medical safety or cybersecurity. The paper needs to discuss the framework's robustness or limitations in transferring across different safety categories.

- Dependence on Reference Model Training Data: The proposed token-level data selection method is highly dependent on the quality and specificity of the reference model training data. However, the paper lacks detailed information regarding the composition, source, and size of the harmful and utility reference datasets ($\mathcal{D}^{h}$ and $\mathcal{D}^{u}$), which are crucial for reproducibility and understanding the framework's effectiveness.

- Potential for Response Disruption and Utility Evaluation: When masking tokens with high token-level scores (safety risk) in the response label during the safe training phase, it is possible that this leads to discontinuous or ill-formed generated responses. The paper should provide a more comprehensive evaluation of the model's general instruction-following utility after TOSS is applied, using widely accepted benchmarks like AlpacaEval and MT-Bench (in addition to the SLIMORCA utility benchmark used), to ensure that the safe fine-tuning process does not cause model degradation or "model collapse."

- Lack of Detail on AI Safety Evaluation Metrics: The paper lacks a detailed introduction and justification for the specific AI safety evaluation metrics used. While the paper mentions safety benchmarks like HEx-PHI and HH, from my understanding, it seems that the description in Appendix C uses evaluation paradigms similar to AlpacaEval.(i.e., LLM-as-a-Judge). This approach is known to have limitations and potential biases in safety evaluation.

1. Considering that the paper's training objective utilizes the **next token prediction pattern** (causal language modeling), a core concern arises regarding the handling of masked tokens. Specifically, if token $y_i$ is identified as a high-risk (harmful) token and is subsequently masked out (i.e., $m_{i}=0$) so that it does not contribute to the loss, the context for the prediction of the next token $y_{i+1}$ still relies on $y_i$ being present in the input sequence (as show in **Line 229 and 286**).This means that the model $f_{\theta}$ is still exposed to the harmful token $y_i$ during the prediction of $y_{i+1}$, which could potentially introduce uncertainty or residual harmful signal into the learned weights, thereby compromising the intended safety enhancement.
Does the paper's current handling method (simply setting the loss weight $m_{i}=0$) adequately mitigate the risk of exposing the model to harmful context for subsequent token predictions? 

2. Are there better optimization strategies that could be explored to fully sever the harmful influence of $y_i$ on the training of $y_{i+1}$? For example, techniques like replacing the high-risk token $y_i$ with a neutral token (e.g., a special [SAFE] or [MASK] token) or completely removing the span of harmful tokens from the input sequence.

3. Distinction from Existing Token-Level Work: We have recently seen several works focusing on token-level filtering or selection, many of which utilize the Shannon entropy $\log P(x)$ (or maximum likelihood loss) derived from the sequence modeling objective. Could the authors explicitly articulate the key differences between the proposed TOSS/TOSS-Pro framework (which uses a loss-difference metric between two specialized reference models) and these contemporary token-level selection methods? Specifically, why is the dual-reference model approach necessary and superior to simpler methods based solely on a single model's loss or entropy (e.g. safety-degraded reference model)?

4. Potential Negative Impact of Token Masking: The paper employs a token-level masking or filtering technique on the training data. Does this token-level masking or filtering of the response labels during the fine-tuning process introduce undesirable side effects on the learned model distribution? Since the model is trained with discontinuous targets (due to masked tokens), is there a risk of degrading the model's fluency or coherence in generation, especially for non-harmful, utility-oriented responses? The paper should provide a dedicated discussion or empirical evidence on this potential trade-off.

summary.value: This paper proposes Token-level data Selection for Safe LLM fine-tuning (TOSS), a novel framework designed to mitigate safety degradation in Large Language Models (LLMs) during fine-tuning on custom datasets. The core innovation is moving from coarse-grained sample-level data selection, which suffers from an unsatisfactory safety-utility trade-off, to a fine-grained token-level approach. TOSS quantifies the safety risk of each token by calculating a loss-difference metric between a safety-degraded model (an expert in unsafe patterns) and a utility-oriented model (an expert in task utility). Tokens with high risk scores are selectively masked (discarded) from the custom dataset before fine-tuning, thereby preserving valuable task-specific information. The paper further introduces TOSS-Pro, a progressive refinement strategy that iteratively updates the safety-degraded model using the most informative harmful samples, which leads to more accurate identification of unsafe tokens and enhanced safeguarding performance. Extensive experiments validate that TOSS and TOSS-Pro achieve a superior trade-off between safety and utility compared to existing sample-level defense methods like SEAL.

strengths.value:
*Originality: The paper makes a highly original contribution by proposing the first token-level data selection framework specifically for safeguarding LLM fine-tuning. The fundamental insight that "the unit of safety degradation is not the sample, but the token" is strongly motivated by a systematic token-level diagnosis, distinguishing this work significantly from prior sample-level methods (e.g., SEAL).
*Quality & Clarity: The proposed methodology, TOSS, is technically sound and clearly articulated. The loss-difference metric is an elegant, intuitive mechanism for quantifying the joint safety-risk and utility-alignment of a token. The introduction of the S(y_{i,j}^{cus})decomposition (Eq. 2) provides excellent clarity on the complementary roles of the two reference models. Furthermore, the empirical evidence, including the main results (Table 1) and comprehensive ablation studies (Figure 4, Tables 3 & 4), strongly supports the claims and validates the effectiveness of the token-level paradigm shift.
*Significance: The work addresses a critical vulnerability in the burgeoning practice of LLM fine-tuning and customization. The superior performance over state-of-the-art baselines, particularly the up to 30% higher win rate on safety benchmarks and 11% on utility benchmarks compared to SEAL on Llama-3-8B-Instruct (Table 1), demonstrates a significant advance in achieving a favorable safety-utility trade-off. The strong transferability result (Table 2) suggests a practical and scalable deployment advantage.

weaknesses.value:
*Computational Cost of Reference Model Training: The core TOSS framework relies on training two full reference models ($f_{\theta^h}$  and $f_{\theta^u}$  ) via SFT, which can be computationally expensive, particularly for much larger LLMs (e.g., Llama-70B). While LoRA fine-tuning is used (Appendix B), the overall process—training two models and then performing token assessment on the entire custom dataset—is significantly more intensive than sample-level filtering that often relies on a single, lighter ranking model (like SEAL's bi-level optimization ranker). The authors should discuss the time complexity and computational overhead, perhaps in relation to the gain, or suggest strategies to reduce this cost (e.g., using smaller reference models or knowledge distillation).
*Hyperparameter Sensitivity of d (Discarding Ratio): While Figure 5 shows robustness across different discarding ratios d, the main results (Table 1) fix d=0.1. The results for d=0.1 show a substantial utility improvement for TOSS (68.37%) over SEAL (57.41%) on Llama-3-8B-Instruct. However, the curves in Figure 5 show that the choice of d is crucial for maximizing utility, which first increases and then decreases. This highlights that d is a critical, potentially fragile, hyperparameter for optimization. A more robust method for automatically or adaptively setting the optimal discarding ratio d (or per-sample local thresholds) would greatly strengthen the framework and reduce deployment complexity.
*Clarity on Progressive Refinement Sample Selection: In TOSS-Pro, the authors select the k most informative harmful samples D_t^s  by finding samples that contain the top-ranked tokens. This is a sample-level selection mechanism built on a token-level score. The paper should elaborate on how a sample is defined to "contain" a top-ranked token in the set of selected samples D_t^s . Does this mean any token in the sample is in the top set, or is there a minimum number/proportion of top tokens required? Clarifying this selection logic is important for reproducibility and understanding how the "higher-quality supervision" is precisely curated

**Q3. The Rationale for Fixing Utility-oriented Model**

We thank the reviewer for this insightful question. We have indeed explored a variant of TOSS-Pro, named TOSS-Pro-utility, in which the utility-oriented model is also progressively refined. Specifically, mirroring the refinement procedure applied to the safety-degraded model, we conduct experiments where the safety-degraded model is kept fixed, and in each iteration we sort all tokens in descending order by their token scores. We then select samples starting from the low-score end, sequentially adding their corresponding sample indices to the refinement set for the utility-oriented model until 5,000 unique samples are collected. This dataset is then used to further update the utility-oriented model.

Our empirical results, illustrated in Table R1 and Appendix D.4, show that after two refinement iterations, the utility performance of this progressively updated utility-oriented method (TOSS-Pro-utility) is almost identical to that of the original TOSS method. Notably, during the initial training of the utility-oriented reference model (i.e., in TOSS), we used only approximately 3% of the full utility dataset, yet this already captures the task-relevant distribution sufficiently well. These results indicate that additional refinement brings negligible performance gains while introducing substantial extra computational cost.

Therefore, we keep the utility-oriented model fixed in TOSS-Pro, as progressive updates do not meaningfully improve utility performance but significantly increase training overhead.

**Q2. Replace High-risk Tokens with Neutral Tokens**

We thank the reviewer for this insightful question. We agree that exploring alternative optimization strategies is an interesting direction. However, as clarified in our response to Question 1, the presence of a masked safety-degrading token $y_{i}$ in the context of a subsequent unmasked token $y_{i+1}$ does not introduce residual harmful signals. Therefore, replacing high-risk tokens with neutral placeholders (e.g., a special \[SAFE] or \[MASK] token) would provide only marginal safety benefits.

Moreover, introducing such neutral tokens may harm model performance in several ways. First, replacing spans with artificial tokens leads to training on unnatural, discontinuous contexts, which can degrade fluency and coherence. Second, these special tokens do not appear in the model’s pretraining or instruction-tuning data, creating a significant distribution shift. Learning the semantics and usage of these new tokens requires additional data and training, increases computational cost, and may negatively impact the model’s general capabilities.

For these reasons, although neutral token replacement is conceptually appealing, its practical drawbacks outweigh its potential benefits. Our simple TOSS strategy avoids these issues while effectively eliminating safety-degrading signals, making it a more efficient and robust solution for safe LLM fine-tuning.

**Q3. Distinction from Existing Token-Level Work**

We thank the reviewer for this insightful question. We are happy to clarify the distinction between our proposed TOSS/TOSS-Pro framework and existing token-level selection approaches that rely on single-model statistics such as Shannon entropy or maximum-likelihood loss.

While prior work \[R10] indeed explores token-level filtering, these methods generally focus on a single goal, most commonly aiming to improve utility by identifying low-probability (high-entropy) tokens from a single base model. Such tokens are viewed as “informative” and beneficial for downstream performance. However, this strategy is fundamentally incompatible with our goal. For our study, we aim to preserve safety performance while maximizing the downstream task utility performance gain through fine-tuning. In this case, both safety-degrading tokens and utility-critical tokens may appear as low-probability under the base model. Consequently, single-model entropy or loss cannot discriminate between harmful and beneficial signals and thus fails to achieve our dual objective.

To address this challenge, we introduce a dual-reference model framework with a loss-difference score. This metric directly compares a token’s likelihood under a safety-degraded model versus a utility-oriented model. Tokens with high scores are those assigned a high probability by the safety-degraded model but a low probability by the utility-oriented model, indicating stronger alignment with harmful generation behavior rather than with utility-driven adaptation. This dual-objective design allows the metric to simultaneously identify and remove safety-degrading tokens while preserving utility-critical tokens, which single-model entropy cannot achieve.

Empirically, we further validate that the dual-reference strategy is not only conceptually necessary but also practically superior. Our ablation study (Figure 4, right) demonstrates that relying solely on the safety-degraded model improves safety but severely harms utility, while relying solely on the utility-oriented model yields no defense (its safety performance collapses similarly to Standard SFT). In contrast, when both the safety-degraded model and the utility-oriented model are jointly used to guide token selection, the resulting fine-tuned model consistently outperforms any single-model variant on both safety and utility metrics, demonstrating the complementary contributions of the two reference models.
